name: caramel frosting
instructions:
A caramel frosting built on a cooked brown-sugar-and-butter caramel base + heavy cream, thickened with powdered sugar, thinned with milk to consistency. Not the smooth pale-tan store-bought caramel look — a deeper, browner, more molasses-forward frosting per the brown-sugar-forward register.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- unsalted butter
- brown sugar (light or dark; dark is deeper)
- heavy whipping cream
- powdered sugar
- milk (for thinning to consistency)
- pinch of salt

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. COOK THE CARAMEL BASE: in a saucepan over medium heat, melt the butter. Add the brown sugar and stir until dissolved. Bring to a gentle simmer.
2. Stir in the heavy cream. Simmer briefly (~2-3 min) until smooth and slightly thickened. Remove from heat.
3. COOL SLIGHTLY: let the caramel base cool for a few minutes before adding powdered sugar — adding it while too hot will make the frosting grainy or too thin.
4. BEAT IN POWDERED SUGAR: whisk in powdered sugar, a bit at a time, until you get the frosting texture you want.
5. THIN WITH MILK TO CONSISTENCY: if the frosting is too thick to spread, thin with milk a tablespoon at a time. If too thin, add more powdered sugar.
6. Pinch of salt to balance the sweetness. Taste and adjust.
notes:
=== BROWN SUGAR + BUTTER + CREAM IS THE CARAMEL BASE ===

The base of this frosting is a proper cooked caramel — butter + brown sugar cooked together, then heavy cream stirred in. Not the artificial-tasting caramel from sweetened-condensed-milk shortcuts. The brown sugar's molasses depth is what gives this frosting its distinctive character; using white sugar would give you a pale, one-note caramel that misses the point.

=== POWDERED SUGAR THICKENS, MILK THINS ===

After the cooked caramel base cools slightly, powdered sugar goes in to thicken it into a spreadable frosting consistency. Milk is the thinner if you overshoot with the powdered sugar. Adjust by feel — this frosting is looser than a stiff buttercream, closer to a poured glaze that sets as it cools.

=== CORN SYRUP — CLASSIC ADDITION FOR ANTI-CRYSTALLIZATION ===

Many classic caramel-frosting recipes call for a small amount of corn syrup (~1 tbsp) added with the brown sugar and butter. Corn syrup is used to prevent the sugar from crystallizing as the caramel cooks and as it cools on the finished cake — it's what keeps a caramel from turning grainy or forming a crystalline crust over time.

Whether you need it depends on your cook: careful stirring, not overheating, and using it same-day means you can often skip. For a frosting that holds well overnight or for a couple of days, corn syrup is real insurance against graininess.

Optional. Not required if you're serving same-day and cooking the caramel carefully.

=== PAIRING — DAD'S OLD FAVORITE ON CHOCOLATE CAKE ===

This frosting on a natural-cocoa chocolate cake (see chocolate-cake) is the optimal pairing — dad's old favorite. The brown-sugar-and-molasses caramel character sits deep against the natural cocoa's acidic-fruity chocolate profile; the two flavors deepen each other rather than competing (as a straight chocolate-buttercream-on-chocolate-cake stack sometimes does).

=== COOL BEFORE ADDING POWDERED SUGAR ===

Don't add powdered sugar while the caramel base is still hot — the sugar will dissolve into it and the frosting won't set thick enough to spread. Wait until the caramel base is warm-to-the-touch (not scalding), then whisk in the powdered sugar.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- cream-cheese-frosting: cream-cheese-based frosting for chocolate-adjacent and lemon-adjacent cakes.
- buttercream-frosting: butter-and-powdered-sugar frosting; the traditional pairing for many american cakes.
- chocolate-cake: the specific cake this caramel frosting is the optimal pairing for.
